clinicalPearls: Hers disease (GSD VI) is an autosomal recessive deficiency of liver glycogen phosphorylase, encoded by PYGL, causing impaired hepatic glycogen breakdown
It is typically a mild hepatic glycogenosis presenting in childhood with hepatomegaly, growth delay, and relatively mild fasting ketotic hypoglycaemia
Biochemical clues include ketosis and mild hypoglycaemia on fasting, with lactate and uric acid usually normal, unlike GSD I
Symptoms and hepatomegaly often improve with age and may become subclinical in adulthood
It overlaps clinically and biochemically with phosphorylase kinase deficiency (GSD IX), and the two are difficult to separate without enzymology or genetics
Management focuses on avoiding prolonged fasting, frequent carbohydrate and protein intake, and uncooked cornstarch to prevent overnight hypoglycaemia and ketosis
Prognosis is generally favourable, though a minority develop hepatic fibrosis or persisting symptoms
reference.pathophysiology: Liver glycogen phosphorylase catalyses the rate-limiting step of glycogenolysis, releasing glucose-1-phosphate from glycogen. In Hers disease, biallelic PYGL variants reduce hepatic phosphorylase activity, so glycogen cannot be efficiently mobilised during fasting. Glycogen accumulates in hepatocytes, producing hepatomegaly, while impaired glucose release causes mild fasting hypoglycaemia with a shift toward ketosis as an alternative fuel. Because gluconeogenesis and lactate handling are preserved, the metabolic derangement is milder than in the more severe hepatic glycogenoses such as GSD I.
additionalDifferentials: Other hepatic glycogen storage diseases (GSD I, III, 0)
Other causes of childhood hepatomegaly with growth delay
additionalInvestigations: Fasting studies documenting mild ketotic hypoglycaemia with normal lactate and uric acid
Liver enzyme phosphorylase activity assay where genetics are inconclusive
Liver ultrasound to assess hepatomegaly and screen for fibrosis
Fasting lipid profile and metabolic screen to distinguish from GSD I and fatty acid oxidation defects
redFlags: Symptomatic hypoglycaemia with seizures or reduced consciousness
Marked lactic acidosis or hyperuricaemia suggesting a more severe glycogenosis such as GSD I
Progressive hepatomegaly or signs of hepatic fibrosis
Poor growth despite dietary measures indicating inadequate metabolic control
reference.prognosis: Hers disease usually has a good prognosis, with hepatomegaly and hypoglycaemia tending to improve through childhood and often resolving in adulthood, though occasional patients develop hepatic fibrosis and require ongoing monitoring.
pitfalls: Assuming severe hypoglycaemia and lactic acidosis, which point instead to GSD I
Trying to separate GSD VI from GSD IX clinically without enzymology or genetics
Underestimating the need for overnight glucose support in symptomatic children
Discharging from follow-up without monitoring for hepatic fibrosis
references: Scriver's Online Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease
GeneReviews: Glycogen Storage Disease Type VI
management: Dietary management is the mainstay: avoid prolonged fasting, provide frequent carbohydrate and protein-containing meals, and give uncooked cornstarch to prevent overnight hypoglycaemia and ketosis
Treat symptomatic hypoglycaemia promptly with rapid-acting carbohydrate and educate families on recognition and home management
Implement a sick-day regimen with increased carbohydrate intake during intercurrent illness to prevent hypoglycaemia and ketosis
Monitor growth and development, and undertake liver ultrasound and enzyme surveillance for the uncommon progression to hepatic fibrosis
Coordinate care with a metabolic dietitian and specialist metabolic team, with dietary liberalisation as symptoms often improve with age
Offer genetic counselling and family testing given autosomal recessive inheritance of PYGL variants
